question: What are the main HTTP methods and what is each used for?
title: HTTP Methods Overview
direct_answer: In a typical REST API, the main HTTP methods describe what a client wants to do with a target resource: `GET` retrieves a representation, `POST` submits data for processing, `PUT` replaces target state, `PATCH` applies change instructions, and `DELETE` removes the URI's current association. `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` support retrieval metadata and capability checks, respectively; `TRACE` and `CONNECT` are specialized protocol methods rather than normal REST resource operations.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `GET` retrieves a representation. `HEAD` asks for the GET response without response content; some content-specific fields may be omitted.
`POST` submits content for resource-specific processing. It often creates a resource, but creation is not its only use.
`PUT` creates or replaces the state at a known target URI; `PATCH` applies change instructions described by a patch format.
`DELETE` removes the target URI's current association. It does not promise that every stored copy, log, or backup is physically erased.
`OPTIONS` describes communication options. `TRACE` runs a diagnostic loop-back, while `CONNECT` establishes a tunnel; TRACE and CONNECT are specialized methods, not normal REST resource operations.
`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` are safe. Those methods plus `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by standard semantics; `CONNECT`, `POST`, and `PATCH` have no general idempotency guarantee.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An HTTP method tells the server what kind of action the client wants for the resource identified by the URI. It is part of the HTTP contract, not just a label on a controller method. Clients, browsers, caches, and gateways use that shared meaning when they send, cache, prefetch, or retry a request.

`GET` retrieves a current representation. `HEAD` asks for the response that GET would produce but does not transfer response content; content-specific fields that require generating the content may be omitted. `OPTIONS` describes communication options for a resource or server. `TRACE` performs a diagnostic loop-back, and `CONNECT` asks a proxy to establish a tunnel. TRACE and CONNECT are specialized protocol methods rather than normal REST controller operations.

`POST` submits content for processing according to the target resource's own rules. `POST /orders` may create an order, but POST can also submit a search, start a job, or run a command. It is broader than “create.”

`PUT` sends the state that should exist at a known target URI. The server creates or replaces that state, and repeating the same PUT has the same intended effect. `PATCH` sends a patch document—a set of changes whose meaning comes from its media type. A PATCH operation can be designed to be idempotent, but the method does not guarantee that property.

`DELETE` asks the server to remove the target URI's current association. It does not define how a database, audit record, or backup must be erased. Method choice also communicates safety and idempotency: safe methods do not ask for a business-state change, while idempotent methods can be repeated with the same intended effect. The implementation must still keep those promises.

sections.title: Why the method is more than a CRUD label
sections.content:
The URI identifies the target resource; the method supplies the request's basic meaning. That split lets an intermediary understand useful properties without knowing the Java code behind the endpoint. A cache can treat GET specially, a crawler can follow safe links, and a client can decide whether a failed request is normally safe to retry.

CRUD is a helpful memory aid, but it is not the definition of the methods. POST is not limited to CREATE, DELETE does not describe a SQL DELETE statement, and PATCH is not simply “PUT with fewer fields.” Headers can further refine the request—for example, `If-Match` can make an update conditional on the resource version—but they cannot contradict the method's core meaning.

An API that uses POST for every action can still transfer data, but it hides information that HTTP could have given to clients and infrastructure.

sections.title: Method semantics at a glance
sections.content:
| Method | Core request | Safe? | Idempotent by method semantics? |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `GET` | Retrieve a representation | Yes | Yes |
| `HEAD` | Ask for the GET response without response content | Yes | Yes |
| `POST` | Process submitted content | No | No guarantee |
| `PUT` | Create or replace target state | No | Yes |
| `PATCH` | Apply a patch document | No | No guarantee |
| `DELETE` | Remove the target URI association | No | Yes |
| `OPTIONS` | Describe communication options | Yes | Yes |
| `TRACE` | Run a diagnostic message loop-back | Yes | Yes |
| `CONNECT` | Establish a tunnel through a proxy | No | No guarantee |

sections.title: Read one order API by method and target
sections.content:
```http
GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

POST /orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 28

{"itemId": 7, "quantity": 2}

DELETE /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
```

The paths identify an order collection or one order. The methods change the meaning: retrieve order 42, submit a new order to the collection, or remove the current association for order 42.

question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
title: PUT vs PATCH
direct_answer: The difference is that `PUT` sends the intended replacement state for a known target URI, while `PATCH` sends instructions for changing its current state. PUT is idempotent by method semantics; PATCH has no general idempotency guarantee.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `PUT` sends the state that should replace the state at a known URI; `PATCH` sends change instructions.
PUT is idempotent. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent, although a particular patch can be repeatable.
The patch media type defines the instructions. JSON Merge Patch and JSON Patch do not use the same document format.
An omitted field in a PUT body does not automatically become `null`; its meaning depends on the resource's representation contract.
Use `If-Match` with an ETag when an update must not overwrite a newer version.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`PUT` and `PATCH` can both update a resource, but their bodies mean different things. PUT carries the state that should exist at the target URI. PATCH carries a patch document that tells the server how to change the current state. The real difference is replacement state versus change instructions, not simply a large body versus a small one.

For `PUT /profiles/42`, a profile representation might contain the name, email, and notification setting that should now describe profile 42. If the target has no current representation, the server can create one there when the contract allows it. Sending the same representation again has the same intended effect, so PUT is idempotent. The API must document what a complete profile representation contains; HTTP does not say that every omitted database column automatically becomes `null`.

For `PATCH /profiles/42`, the body follows a patch media type. A JSON Merge Patch such as `{"displayName":"Ada"}` replaces that member and leaves unmentioned members unchanged; a `null` member normally requests removal. JSON Patch uses operations such as `replace`, `remove`, and `add`. Setting a value can be repeatable, while incrementing a counter or appending an item can apply the change twice. PATCH therefore has no method-wide idempotency guarantee.

Choose PUT when the client can describe the intended target state and replacement is the API contract. Choose PATCH when the client needs to send a defined set of changes. Either request can overwrite a newer edit, so `If-Match` with an ETag can make the update fail with `412 Precondition Failed` when the client's version is stale. Both methods still need authorization and validation.

PATCH carries a patch document that tells the server how to change the current state. The real difference is replacement state versus change instructions, not simply a large body versus a small one.

sections.title: Replacement, patch format, and version checks solve different problems
sections.content:
PUT's idempotency comes from the HTTP meaning of the method, not from a Spring annotation. An endpoint that treats repeated PUT requests as “increment this value” breaks that meaning. The request representation describes the target state, but the API still decides which fields belong to that representation, which fields are server-managed, and whether a missing field is invalid or has a documented default.

PATCH leaves the change language to the patch media type. JSON Merge Patch treats object members as replacements and uses `null` to remove a member, which makes a stored JSON null difficult to express for that member. JSON Patch uses an ordered list of operations and paths. A server must apply a PATCH document atomically: it applies the complete change or none of it, rather than exposing a half-updated resource.

A conditional request solves another problem. `If-Match` says “apply this update only if the current ETag is one of these values.” It protects both PUT and PATCH from silently replacing work that another client saved after this client last read the resource.

sections.title: Compare the update contracts
sections.content:
| Question | `PUT` | `PATCH` |
|---|---|---|
| What does the body mean? | Intended target state | Change instructions |
| Idempotent by method definition? | Yes | No guarantee |
| Common body | Resource representation | JSON Patch, JSON Merge Patch, or another documented patch format |
| Can it create at target URI? | Yes, when the server accepts creation there | Possible for some patch formats and server contracts |
| Can it overwrite a newer edit? | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: The same profile expressed as state or as a change
sections.content:
A replacement request sends the intended profile state:

```http
PUT /profiles/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 64
If-Match: "profile-v12"

{"displayName":"Ada L.","email":"ada@example.com","alerts":true}
```

A partial-change request sends a patch document:

```http
PATCH /profiles/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json
Content-Length: 24
If-Match: "profile-v12"

{"displayName":"Ada L."}
```

Both requests are conditional on version 12. PUT supplies the intended profile state; PATCH supplies one change. A stale request fails instead of silently replacing a newer edit.

sections.title: Test a retry twice
sections.content: Apply each JSON Patch document twice to the same starting state. `[{"op":"replace","path":"/status","value":"shipped"}]` reaches the same state, while `[{"op":"add","path":"/tags/-","value":"priority"}]` may append the value twice. PATCH still has no method-wide idempotency guarantee.

question: How do you map HTTP methods to Spring Boot controller annotations?
title: HTTP Methods in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring MVC maps methods with `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping`. A controller still has to implement the matching HTTP semantics, validate input, call application logic, and return an appropriate status and representation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Map GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE with `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping`.
Use class-level `@RequestMapping` for a shared path such as `/orders`, then give each method its remaining path.
Use `@RestController` when controller return values should be written to the HTTP response body.
Read path identifiers with `@PathVariable`, query controls with `@RequestParam`, and request content with `@RequestBody`.
Use `@Valid` to request Bean Validation of a constrained DTO and `ResponseEntity` when status or headers need explicit control.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In Spring MVC, a mapping annotation connects an HTTP method and path to one controller method. `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping` are method-specific shortcuts for `@RequestMapping`. A class-level `@RequestMapping("/orders")` can hold the common path, while each method adds its own path and HTTP method.

The method parameters say where input comes from. `@PathVariable long id` reads the `42` in `/orders/42`. `@RequestParam String status` reads a query value such as `?status=paid`. `@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request` asks an HTTP message converter, commonly backed by Jackson for JSON, to create the DTO. Adding `@Valid` runs Bean Validation before normal controller logic when validation is configured.

Because `@RestController` includes response-body handling, returning an `OrderResponse` normally serializes that DTO into the response. Use `ResponseEntity` when the result needs an explicit status or headers. For a successful create, `return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);` sends `201 Created`, a `Location` header, and the created representation. A delete with nothing to return can use a 204 response instead.

The annotation chooses the handler; it does not make the endpoint correct. A method marked `@GetMapping` must still avoid a requested state change, and a `@PutMapping` implementation must preserve PUT's idempotent replacement meaning. Keep HTTP translation in the controller, call a service for business work, and use request and response DTOs instead of exposing persistence entities as the public contract.

beats.spokenText: In Spring MVC, a mapping annotation connects an HTTP method and path to one controller method. `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping` are method-specific shortcuts for `@RequestMapping`. sections.title: What happens after a mapped request arrives
sections.content:
Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` receives the request. Handler mapping compares the HTTP method, path, requested media types, and other mapping conditions to select one controller method. If the path matches but the HTTP method is not allowed, the request must not be sent to a differently annotated handler.

After a handler is selected, argument resolvers read path and query values. An `HttpMessageConverter` reads the request body; in a typical Spring Boot JSON API, Jackson converts JSON into the request DTO. When the parameter has `@Valid` and Bean Validation is available, invalid input can be rejected before the controller calls its service.

On the way back, a return-value handler and message converter build the HTTP response. A plain object from a `@RestController` is normally written as response content. `ResponseEntity` is useful when the controller must also choose a status or add headers such as `Location`. The mapping starts the request flow; the controller still has to return the correct HTTP result and keep business work in an application service.

sections.title: Spring MVC request path
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[HTTP
request] --> B[Match method
and path] B --> C[Bind input
and validate] C -- valid --> D[Controller
and service] D --> E[HTTP
response] C -- invalid --> F[Validation
error] ```

question: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
title: Idempotency in HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Idempotency means that several identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as one request. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent by method semantics; `POST` and `PATCH` have no general idempotency guarantee.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Idempotency means one identical request or several have the same intended server effect.
`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent by method semantics.
`POST` and `PATCH` have no general idempotency guarantee, although a particular operation can add one.
The responses may differ. A repeated DELETE can return a different status while the intended final state is still ‘absent.’
Every safe method is idempotent, but idempotent methods such as PUT and DELETE are not safe.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An HTTP method is idempotent when several identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as one request. It does not mean the responses must be identical or that the server performs no internal work. A server may log every attempt; the requested resource effect is what must not be applied again.

HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as safe and therefore idempotent. `PUT` and `DELETE` are also idempotent even though they request a state change. `POST` and `PATCH` have no general idempotency guarantee. For example, setting a status to `paid` can reach the same state twice, while adding ten credits repeats the change.

Suppose `DELETE /orders/42` succeeds but the response is lost. A retry might return `404 Not Found` because the order is already absent, yet the intended final state is still the same. Repeating the same `PUT /settings/42` representation should likewise leave the same settings. Different responses do not by themselves make a method non-idempotent.

POST does not provide an idempotency guarantee, so retrying `POST /payments` blindly can create a duplicate payment. An API can add an idempotency-key contract: the same key and the same request identify one logical operation, while reusing the key with different content should be rejected. This is behavior supplied by the API, not by POST itself.

beats.cue: Define idempotency by the intended server effect
beats.spokenText: An HTTP method is idempotent when several identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as one request. It does not mean the responses must be identical or that the server performs no internal work. A server may log every attempt; the requested resource effect is what must not be applied again.

beats.cue: Group the standard methods by their protocol guarantee
beats.spokenText: HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as safe and therefore idempotent. `PUT` and `DELETE` are also idempotent even though they request a state change. `POST` and `PATCH` have no general idempotency guarantee. For example, setting a status to `paid` can reach the same state twice, while adding ten credits repeats the change.

items.label: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE
items.detail: The client asks for information or communication options, not a business-state change.

items.label: PUT and DELETE
items.detail: They change target state, but repeating the same request keeps the same intended effect.

items.label: POST and PATCH
items.detail: The endpoint can define retry-safe behavior, but the method name does not promise it.

beats.cue: Use a lost response to distinguish effect from response
beats.spokenText: Suppose `DELETE /orders/42` succeeds but the response is lost. A retry might return `404 Not Found` because the order is already absent, yet the intended final state is still the same. Repeating the same `PUT /settings/42` representation should likewise leave the same settings. Different responses do not by themselves make a method non-idempotent.

beats.cue: Show how a non-idempotent method can add an application contract
beats.spokenText: POST does not provide an idempotency guarantee, so retrying `POST /payments` blindly can create a duplicate payment. An API can add an idempotency-key contract: the same key and the same request identify one logical operation, while reusing the key with different content should be rejected. This is behavior supplied by the API, not by POST itself.
beats.recallRule: Idempotency is sameness of intended effect; method semantics provide the default, while a POST or PATCH operation needs an explicit application contract before retries are safe.

sections.title: Retry safety needs an operation identity
sections.content:
A network can lose the response after the server commits the change. From the client, that looks the same as a request the server never received. Idempotent method semantics let the request be repeated without repeating the intended effect.

An API can define an idempotency key as its own contract for a non-idempotent operation. That contract must explain what counts as the same request, how long a key is remembered, what a completed retry receives, and what happens while the first request is still running. Those rules are application-defined; POST and RFC 9110 do not supply them. The implementation also has to stop two concurrent requests with the same key from both being treated as new.

Conditional requests solve a different problem. `If-Match` prevents applying a change to an unexpected version, while an application-defined idempotency key can identify a repeated logical operation.

sections.title: A response is lost, then the client retries
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as API
  participant S as Idempotency store
  C->>A: POST /payments (key K, request R)
  A->>S: atomically reserve K for fingerprint(R)
  A->>A: create payment P
  A->>S: store completed response for K
  A--xC: response lost
  C->>A: retry same K and R
  A->>S: load completed K
  A-->>C: return original outcome, no second payment
```

sections.title: The key represents one logical operation
sections.content:
```http
POST /payments HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 54
Idempotency-Key: 82c35d3e-8d70-44f9-aaf3-24ad14d8e615

{"orderId": "O-42", "amount": 1999, "currency": "INR"}
```

A retry uses the same key only for the same logical request. The API must define expiry, mismatch, in-progress, and failure behavior.

sections.title: Method guarantee versus endpoint behavior
sections.content: A JSON Patch `replace` operation can be repeatable, while an `add` operation using the array-end path `/-` may append twice. A particular PATCH can behave idempotently, but PATCH still has no method-wide idempotency guarantee.

question: What are safe HTTP methods and why does the distinction matter?
title: Safe HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Safe HTTP methods are methods whose defined request semantics are essentially read-only: `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE`. They may still cause incidental work such as access logging; safety means the client did not ask for an application-state change.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The standard safe methods are `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE`.
Safe means the client did not request an application-state change; it does not mean zero server activity.
Every safe method is idempotent, but an idempotent method such as `DELETE` is not safe.
Automated agents, prefetchers, crawlers, and caches rely on safe-method semantics.
Never hide a destructive action behind a GET link or query parameter.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A safe HTTP method has essentially read-only request semantics: the client asks for information or communication options and does not ask the server to change application state. HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as safe. Safety describes the method contract, not whether the server performs absolutely no internal work.

A safe request may write an access log, update a metric, or fill a cache. Those effects happen while serving the read; they are not the business action requested by the client. Cancelling an order, charging the customer for an order, or reducing inventory is different because it changes application state on the client's behalf and must not be hidden inside GET.

Browsers can prefetch links, crawlers can follow them, and caches can retrieve them automatically. If `GET /orders/42?cancel=true` cancels an order, an automated reader can cause data loss simply by following a URI. The cancellation needs an unsafe operation such as `POST /orders/42/cancellation` or a documented state update, together with the normal authorization and retry rules.

Every safe method is also idempotent, but the reverse is not true. `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by method semantics because repeating them has the same intended effect, yet they are not safe because they request a change. `TRACE` is standardized as safe but is often disabled; a method can be safe by semantics without every server choosing to support it.

beats.cue: Define safety from the effect requested by the client
beats.spokenText: A safe HTTP method has essentially read-only request semantics: the client asks for information or communication options and does not ask the server to change application state. HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as safe. Safety describes the method contract, not whether the server performs absolutely no internal work.

beats.cue: Separate incidental server work from a requested business action
beats.spokenText: A safe request may write an access log, update a metric, or fill a cache. Those effects happen while serving the read; they are not the business action requested by the client. Cancelling an order, charging the customer for an order, or reducing inventory is different because it changes application state on the client's behalf and must not be hidden inside GET.

beats.cue: Show why crawlers and prefetchers depend on the distinction
beats.spokenText: Browsers can prefetch links, crawlers can follow them, and caches can retrieve them automatically. If `GET /orders/42?cancel=true` cancels an order, an automated reader can cause data loss simply by following a URI. The cancellation needs an unsafe operation such as `POST /orders/42/cancellation` or a documented state update, together with the normal authorization and retry rules.

items.label: GET /orders/42
items.detail: A crawler or prefetcher may retrieve it without asking to change the order.

items.label: GET /orders/42?cancel=true
items.detail: A read-shaped request secretly performs a destructive business action.

items.label: POST /orders/42/cancellation
items.detail: The method makes the requested state change visible to clients and controls.

beats.cue: Distinguish safety from idempotency and availability
beats.spokenText: Every safe method is also idempotent, but the reverse is not true. `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by method semantics because repeating them has the same intended effect, yet they are not safe because they request a change. `TRACE` is standardized as safe but is often disabled; a method can be safe by semantics without every server choosing to support it.
beats.recallRule: Ask what effect the client requested: information is safe, while a requested business-state change is unsafe even when it can be repeated idempotently.

sections.title: The controller must keep the method's promise
sections.content:
Safety is judged by the effect the client requests, not by the annotation or function name. A `@GetMapping` handler that calls cancellation logic is still an unsafe operation wearing a GET label. Logging the read is different because the client did not ask for the log entry as the result of the request.

At the HTTP boundary, keep reads and commands separate. A link or automated reader can retrieve an order with GET without changing it. Cancellation gets its own unsafe endpoint, where the API can apply authorization, validation, and any retry rule required by that command.

A useful test records the order state, calls the GET endpoint, and proves the state did not change. A separate test calls the cancellation endpoint and checks the intended transition. This tests the behavioral promise instead of trusting the annotation alone.

sections.title: Safety and idempotency are different axes
sections.content:
| Method group | Safe? | Idempotent? | Example |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE` | Yes | Yes | Read or inspect capabilities |
| `PUT`, `DELETE` | No | Yes | Replace or remove target state |
| `POST`, `PATCH` | No | No guarantee | Process content or apply a patch |
